topics.topic: Exact CPython 3.12 release artifact and digest pinned by the release
questions: What concrete artifact does the Python version's required digest identify, so installation can compare it and Required test 1 can vary it?
Which exact CPython 3.12 patch release does the first Registry release name and install?

quotes:
1. A release names every dependency it runs with, at an exact version, with
   its digest: every Python package, direct or transitive, by the digest of
   its distribution file; the Python version; and the base image of VM
   Platform's Registry environment by its digest, which fixes the system
   libraries and the store's engine. Tools used only to build or test are not
   dependencies of the running instance.

6. A release runs on Linux and on no other host — the kernel that runs
   Registry's process is Linux's and so is the base image around it — no
   version named, and its Python is CPython 3.12 (owner, 2026-11-25).

A20 and A21 have no runtime owner. A20 is a property of the release — which
dependencies it names and installs — made and checked by the release process,
which Registry does not manage (Explicit exclusions); A21 is an evidence record
checked by `design_lint --state 2`. `30_trace.json` records both as such.
judgement.why: State 2 fixes the exact-version-and-digest guarantee and the CPython 3.12 family, while release generation must select the patch release and digest-bearing runtime artifact and deployment must compare the installed artifact with that declaration.
options: Digest a separately distributed CPython runtime artifact.
Use the base-image digest as the Python runtime's digest because the interpreter is supplied by that image.
Digest the installed interpreter binary or runtime tree.
Select and pin one current supported CPython 3.12 patch release when the release is generated.
Fix a particular CPython 3.12 patch release in the design until a new design decision changes it.
consequences: A separate runtime artifact gives Python an independently verifiable identity but requires deployment to install or expose that artifact.
Reusing the base-image digest makes the Python and base-image digest cases identical.
Digesting an installed binary or tree requires a canonical scope and may vary with packaging details.
Selecting the patch during generation permits patched 3.12 releases while keeping each produced release reproducible.
Fixing the patch in design requires a design change for maintenance updates.

topics.topic: Whether removed file-opening and backup-flushing semantics remain part of the host support boundary
questions: Is the displayed list exhaustive, so opening a file without following a link is no longer a host semantic on which Registry may rely and the files_artifacts guarantees must hold without it, or is that semantic still an implicit reason to declare a Linux or file system unsupported?

Did the change intentionally remove opening a file without following a link and flushing a backup from the facilities whose non-Linux behaviour makes a host unsupported, or must those facilities remain in A20 for the claim that no guarantee or outcome changed to be true?

quotes:
6. A release runs on Linux and on no other host — the kernel that runs
   Registry's process is Linux's and so is the base image around it — no
   version named, and its Python is CPython 3.12 (owner, 2026-11-25). Another system, or a Linux or
   file system on which a call Registry's rules rely on — binding a listener
   exclusively and to IPv6 alone (A17), renaming a file into place (A17,
   A18) — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither
   tests for it nor defines what it does there.

Under
files_artifacts (A17, A18), renaming the store and a backup into place is
Linux's. Under concurrency (A17), binding each listener exclusively and to
IPv6 alone is Linux's.

Registry follows no link and enters no directory
   there.

No guarantee
weakened: rule 6 names the host they were written for. No right,

topics.topic: Linux documentation baseline and observable semantics that determine support
questions: Which Linux documentation baseline and which observable binding, IPv6-only, and rename semantics decide whether a Linux kernel or filesystem is supported?

quotes:
Another system, or a Linux or

   exclusively and to IPv6 alone (A17), renaming a file into place (A17,
   A18) — does not act as Linux documents it, is unsupported: Registry neither

judgement.why: The text names neither a documentation baseline nor direct observable semantics, so it is impossible to prove from the texts which classification of the reviewer's hypothetical host violates the support rule.
judgement.owner_question: Which documentation baseline or directly stated observable binding, IPv6-only and rename semantics determine whether a Linux kernel or file system is supported?
options: Name a specific Linux man-pages or kernel-documentation baseline and the required observable semantics.
Define the required observable semantics directly without pinning a documentation version.
Declare every Linux implementation supported and leave behavioural differences outside Registry's guarantees.
consequences: A pinned documentation baseline makes support classification version-dependent.
Direct observable semantics make the support boundary testable without interpreting changing documentation.
Supporting every Linux implementation would remove the present unsupported-host boundary and could weaken guarantees resting on binding or rename behaviour.

topics.topic: Non-Linux host installation behavior and support status
questions: On a host whose kernel is not Linux's, must installation fail with no instance starting as Required test 7 says, or is Registry's behaviour untested and undefined because that host is “another system”?

quotes:
5. Rules 1–4 and 6 are kept by the release process and its installation,
   which Registry does not manage (00_product.md, Explicit exclusions): they
   make the release, name its dependencies and host and install them, and
   Registry's own code reads none of it (owner, 2026-11-24).

7. Installing a release on a host whose kernel is not Linux's fails, and no
   instance of it starts (rule 6).
judgement.why: P1 already judged the same non-Linux installation and no-start question on unchanged passages, distinguishing the required outcome from its deployment enforcement mechanism.
options: The installer checks the target kernel and aborts before installation or launch, with every start path required to pass through it.
The deployment platform schedules the release only on Linux kernels and rejects incompatible targets, including recovery and manual-start paths.
A launch supervisor checks the actual kernel before every process start and reports an incompatible target as installation failure.
consequences: Installer enforcement is bypassable unless every installation and copied-release start path is covered.
Platform enforcement must identify the kernel actually running Registry rather than only the build image.
Launch-time enforcement covers copied or previously installed releases but must preserve the required installation-failure outcome without moving the check into Registry code.

author_guidance: Before editing, identify the decision's owning state from the phase purpose, question_scope and layer obligations, then choose a disposition for each topic that awaits one.
fixed: repair a decision the owning state must make; do not add later-layer implementation choices merely to close a topic. Record the fix commit and review the changed text once.

carried: name the receiving layer and use --what to preserve the choice, its options and consequences, and the required guarantee every option must keep. Decide any guarantee owned here before carrying its execution onward.
accepted: explain why the remaining choice is permitted. Bring an unresolved product choice to the owner with its options and consequences; absence of a quoted requirement does not decide it.
contradiction and standard_violation take no disposition: repair the offending text in its owning state and review the change. Deterministic transition findings must also close through their checks.
State 2: decide required results and constraints, including necessary refusal precedence; carry test mechanisms, exact contracts and deployment procedures to their owners.
